chunks: Why CMOS is used everywhere. The question: Why are these so often used?
CMOS dominates because it uses almost no power while it is sitting still.
In each gate (a tiny logic circuit), one transistor is always off, so there is no steady path from the supply to ground. Energy is spent only when a signal changes.
That makes it practical to put billions of gates on one chip.
Picture a water gate in a canal that has two doors: an upper door and a lower door. They are never open together.
Water only moves in a burst when you swap which door is open, and it sits still the rest of the time. Older logic was like leaving a tap trickling whenever the output was low.
The cost of CMOS is that every swap costs a burst, so faster switching uses more power.
In resistor-load (or depletion-load) NMOS logic, whenever the input is high the transistor is on and current flows straight from V DD through R L to ground for as long as the output stays low.
Static power: power used while nothing is changing. In CMOS, only leakage. Dynamic power: power used when signals change, about CV squared each cycle.
C is the capacitance being charged (how much charge a wire or input soaks up per volt) and V is the supply. Leakage: a tiny current that flows even when a transistor is off.
Noise margin: how much unwanted voltage a logic level can tolerate before it is misread. Fan-out: how many inputs one output drives.
Take one CMOS inverter whose output is held high, then held low. Both times one transistor is off, so no current flows from supply to ground.
It only draws energy at the moment it changes. Say it drives a 1 fF load (a femtofarad, a tiny capacitance) at 1 volts.
Each full cycle costs about CV squared equals 1 fF times 1 volts squared equals 1 fJ. That is the whole idea.
"Mainly power. In CMOS the PMOS pull-up and NMOS pull-down are complementary, so one is always off and there's no static current, only leakage.
You pay energy only when a node switches, about CV squared per cycle.
On top of that, outputs swing rail to rail for big noise margins, inputs are gates that draw no DC current so fan-out is huge, and MOSFETs scale and integrate densely.
The costs are dynamic power at high frequency, leakage at small nodes and ESD sensitivity."
